eligibility_note: Meets all criteria: own panel/cross-section regressions, internet/mobile payments exposure, 62-155 economies, outcomes in poverty/distribution and labour market. Fintech credit and e-payments are context exposures, but internet use alone qualifies.

sample_corrections.n_economies: Correct as recorded (148 stated; Table 7 70, Table 8 62, Table 9 64, Table 10 147, Table 11 148, Table 12 95, Tables 13-14 155). Text says 148 countries but cross-section tables report 155, an inconsistency in the paper.
sample_corrections.years: Correct as recorded (text: 'pooled data of 148 countries for 14 years (from 2008 to 2021)'; Table 7 and 12 2013-2019; Table 8 2008-2019; Table 9 and 11 2008-2020; Table 10 2008-2019; Tables 13-14 year 2021).

results.correction: Option labels are off by one. In Table 7 the INTRNT row is blank in option I: -0.17*** (t=-4.32) is option II, -0.13** (t=-2.30) is option III, -0.22*** (t=-5.67) option IV, -0.22*** (t=-5.68) option V. Direction (negative) and magnitudes are right.

results.quote: Table 11 FINTCBIG -0.32 (-0.58); Table 10 FINTCBIG 1.08 (0.95), 1.65 (1.46); text: FINTCBIG 'are not significant'

results.correction: Numbers and t-values match Table 12 (0.99** (2.13), 0.99*** (3.11), 1.15*** (3.71), 0.86*** (2.68)), but only options I-II are per-capita income growth; options IV-V are GDP growth (header 'Per Capita Income Growth' I-III, 'GDP Growth' IV-V). Option III has no FINTCBIG coefficient.
results.quote: Table 12 header: 'Per Capita Income Growth' (I-III), 'GDP Growth' (IV-V); FINTCBIG 0.99**, 0.99***, 1.15***, 0.86***

results.correction: Table 13 also has a 30PSBL40 (lowest 40% income group) version: ELCPMT 0.18** (2.90), CRCRD 0.45*** (5.45); outcome is a perception, not a living-standard measure.
results.quote: Table 13 ELCPMT 0.24*** (3.86); CRCRD 0.48*** (5.83); No. of Countries 155; Year 2021

heterogeneity.correction: No interaction or income-group subsample regression; descriptive tables only. Table 13-14 do include a regression for the bottom-40% income group (30PSBL40) within countries, which the record does not mention.
heterogeneity.quote: 'These last two equations have been estimated for lowest 40 percent income group separately.' (Section 4)

income_group_note: No regression results by World Bank income group; 'not reported' is right. Only descriptive Tables 1-4 by region/high-middle income.

risk_of_bias.confounding_reverse_causation: agree: authors state simultaneity (Figs 1-2) but use no instrument or lag, causal wording ('alleviate poverty'), controls vary by option.
risk_of_bias.exposure_measurement: agree: internet use is a standard measure; Findex-based mobile/e-payment and sparse fintech credit data are weaker (moderate).
risk_of_bias.selection_of_countries_years: agree: availability-driven unbalanced samples varying from 62 to 155 economies, countries not listed (moderate).
risk_of_bias.outcome_measurement: agree: sparse survey poverty/Gini and perception outcomes (moderate).
risk_of_bias.specification: agree: many equations and options with different regressors, unclear FE, adj R2 as low as 0.02-0.05 (serious could be argued, moderate would be too lenient).
risk_of_bias.selective_reporting: agree: abstract/conclusion claim 'robust' and employment effects although coefficients lose significance across options and FINTCBIG is insignificant for labour outcomes (serious).
risk_of_bias.why: Serious is consistent with the guide: causal language, acknowledged simultaneity, no identification strategy.

problems: No invention or paper mix-up found. Minor errors: Table 7 option labels for INTRNT (I vs II, II vs III); Table 12 dependent variable differs between options (per-capita income growth vs GDP growth). Record omits the 30PSBL40 (bottom-40%) estimates in Table 13. Record's claim 'mobile payment lowers Gini' as contradicted by Table 8 is slightly loose: text only says MBLPMT was tested on Gini and Table 8 shows no MBLPMT, which is right.

eligibility_note: Borderline but acceptable: own growth-accounting and calibrated equilibrium decompositions (own computation of ICT-specific technical change from quality-adjusted prices), 10 high-income economies, outcome output/productivity. No regression and no uncertainty measures; exposure is ICT investment-specific technical change, not adoption.

sample_corrections.unit: Country-level period averages 1980-2010 (Tables 1-7 report one value per country), not a country-year panel.
sample_corrections.n_economies: 10 confirmed (AUT, DEN, FIN, GER, ITA, NLD, SPA, SWE, U.K., U.S.)

results.quote: Table 5 ICT (a) contribution: AUT 0.24, DEN 0.39, FIN 0.24, GER 0.22, ITA 0.28, NLD 0.27, SPA 0.27, SWE 0.33, U.K. 0.28, U.S. 0.31; share 9.2-18.9%

results.correction: Direction should be 'mixed', not 'null': no cross-country dependence of TFP on ICT intensity, but a strong negative time-series correlation between ICT growth and TFP growth in high-ICT-growth countries (no coefficient given). Also note TFP is a residual in an accounting identity, not an estimated effect.
results.quote: 'we do find an ordinate pattern between TFP and ICT when looking at the time dimension... strong negative correlation' (Section 3, p.1196)

heterogeneity.correction: Table 7 shows non-ICT contribution above ICT in every country (e.g., 0.85 vs 0.53 in Germany), while Table 5 has ICT above non-ICT in 8 of 10 countries; 'similar magnitude' is the authors' wording.
heterogeneity.quote: 'contributions to growth from ICT and non-ICT assets technical change are of similar magnitude for all countries' (Conclusions, p.1197)

income_group_note: Only high-income economies; 0.41-0.67 pp per year of labour productivity growth (Table 7) is correct.

risk_of_bias.confounding_reverse_causation: agree: accounting decomposition with calibrated weights; no treatment of endogeneity of ICT investment, 'determinants' wording (serious).
risk_of_bias.exposure_measurement: agree: ICT technical change inferred from quality-adjusted prices, with non-ICT prices built from US adjustments; not adoption (moderate).
risk_of_bias.selection_of_countries_years: agree: ten high-income countries chosen by data availability (moderate).
risk_of_bias.outcome_measurement: agree: EU KLEMS national accounts GDP and productivity (low).
risk_of_bias.specification: agree: results highly method dependent (TFP negative in 7 of 10 countries under Hulten; authors admit sensitivity), moderate is acceptable though serious is arguable.
risk_of_bias.selective_reporting: agree: all methods and countries reported (low); authors do not give uncertainty.
risk_of_bias.why: Serious reflects that the measure captures a supply-side technical-change component and the paper interprets contributions as determinants without any strategy for endogeneity.

problems: No invention found. Record unit should be country-period averages, and result 4 direction should be mixed. The paper's own Hulten ISTC range is stated inconsistently (text 0.86-1.23 pp vs 0.68-1.25 in Section 3; Table 6 gives 0.84-1.23), but the record does not use these figures.

eligibility_note: Meets all: own AMG/MG estimation, ICT investment exposure, 17 EU economies, TFP outcome. Manufacturing only, all high income or near (mostly EU members).

sample_corrections.n_economies: 17 confirmed. Hungary appears in text (p.8-9) and in the sector figures but not in the list of 17 or the EU-12 Figure 1.
sample_corrections.unit: industry-country-year (13 manufacturing sectors); Table 1 N=1322 (MG) and 1106 (AMG), Table 2 N=1158

results.quote: Table 1 AMG Robust: Ln ITC .00817** (.00414); text: 'positively correlated to TFP, although the effect is small in economic terms'

results.correction: Column 1 is calculated (accounting) TFP, column 2 estimated TFP.

heterogeneity.correction: Text only keeps the three groups; no group-specific ICT coefficients are reported.
heterogeneity.quote: 'we keep the three distinct groups of EU members, core, South and East' (Section 3)

income_group_note: No income-group or EU-group results; pooled estimates only.

risk_of_bias.confounding_reverse_causation: agree: AMG handles common factors but ICT investment is not instrumented or lagged and the authors recommend 'widen the use of ITCs'; authors concede reverse-causation reading for wages only.
risk_of_bias.exposure_measurement: agree: ICT investment definition, unit and source not reported (moderate).
risk_of_bias.selection_of_countries_years: agree: 17 countries by data availability, manufacturing only, ends 2007 (moderate).
risk_of_bias.outcome_measurement: agree: TFP is a model-based generated regressor with no correction for estimation error (moderate).
risk_of_bias.specification: agree: R&D and structural funds dropped when insignificant, trend choices, two-step estimation (moderate).
risk_of_bias.selective_reporting: agree: abstract says human capital 'plays a role' though Table 1 coefficients insignificant (it is significant in Table 2 first differences, D.ln Human Capital .00272**); robustness checks not shown (moderate).
risk_of_bias.why: Serious is consistent: causal policy wording and no identification for ICT.

problems: No invention found. Minor: record says Hungary appears in 'text and figures' (verified). The record's selective-reporting point about human capital should note Table 2 shows a significant first-difference coefficient.

eligibility_note: Meets all: LSDV panel regressions, ICT spending and internet users, 21 EU economies, labour productivity outcome, CEE vs WE comparison.

sample_corrections.n_economies: 21 confirmed (7 CEE + 14 WE); excluded CY, EE, LV, LT, LU, MT
sample_corrections.income_groups_covered: Paper gives no World Bank income classification; CEE vs WE only

results.correction: Whether dependent variable is in logs is not clear (equation 4 not legible), so the percent interpretation is an assumption.
Direction 'mixed' is a judgement; only 2000-2007 is significant.
2000-2007 coefficient -0.038 (0.019) has t of about 2.0 but carries no star.

heterogeneity.correction: Difference between CEE and WE is not tested formally.
The 2000-2007 significant 'education' variable is gross enrolment (Edu 0.013***), not public education spending (EduS 0.034 ns).

income_group_note: Paper reports only CEE vs WE splits; the numbers cited (WE 0.058*, internet 0.002***; CEE 0.150***) are right, but mapping to World Bank income groups (BG, RO as upper-middle) is not in the paper.

risk_of_bias.confounding_reverse_causation: agree: static LSDV on levels, no instruments, lags or unit-root checks; 'impact' language.
risk_of_bias.exposure_measurement: agree: ICT spending as % GDP labelled 'ICT capital', WITSA editions 2002, 2006, 2010 used for annual data (moderate).
risk_of_bias.selection_of_countries_years: agree: 21 EU members after dropping six for data; small sub-samples (moderate).
risk_of_bias.outcome_measurement: agree: Total Economy Database labour productivity per hour (low).
risk_of_bias.specification: agree: nine regressors with 28-112 obs in sub-periods, no clustering, no robustness section, equations garbled in text (moderate).
risk_of_bias.selective_reporting: agree: text states R&D positive and significant for CEE in 1990s and after crisis (conclusion p.218) but Table 5 shows RDS 0.046 (0.025) and 0.029 (0.019) without stars; 'RDS... only significant for whole sample' while Table 4 shows -0.064*** for WE and whole sample only -0.024 with a dot (moderate).
risk_of_bias.why: Serious: causal wording with no strategy for endogeneity of ICT spending.

problems: No invention found. Record statements verified, including the conflicts between text and tables on R&D (log(RDS) CEE 0.046/0.043/0.029 not starred). The note that Bulgaria and Romania were upper-middle is external to the paper.
